claim: ON and OFF pathways encode increases or decreases of a stimulus from a common input.
source: ON and OFF pathways, for example, encode increases or decreases of a stimulus from a common input.
evidence: This is a general statement about sensory processing presented in the abstract and introduction.

claim: The ON/OFF pathway split is thought to occur at individual synaptic connections through a sign-inverting synapse in one of the pathways.
source: This ON/OFF pathway split is thought to occur at individual synaptic connections through a sign-inverting synapse in one of the pathways.
evidence: This represents the prevailing model in the field that the authors are challenging.

claim: ON selectivity is a multisynaptic process in the Drosophila visual system.
source: Here, we show that ON selectivity is a multisynaptic process in the Drosophila visual system.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental results throughout the manuscript.

claim: Both glutamatergic inhibition through GluClα and GABAergic inhibition through Rdl mediate ON responses.
source: A pharmacogenetics approach demonstrates that both glutamatergic inhibition through GluClα and GABAergic inhibition through Rdl mediate ON responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated through pharmacological experiments with PTX and PTX-insensitive alleles shown in Figures 2, 4, and 6.

claim: Neurons postsynaptic to the glutamatergic ON pathway input L1 lose all responses in GluClα mutants.
source: Although neurons postsynaptic to the glutamatergic ON pathway input L1 lose all responses in GluClα mutants, they are resistant to a cell-type-specific loss of GluClα.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 where full GluClα mutants lose all ON responses but cell-type-specific knockdowns do not.

claim: Neurons postsynaptic to L1 are resistant to a cell-type-specific loss of GluClα.
source: Although neurons postsynaptic to the glutamatergic ON pathway input L1 lose all responses in GluClα mutants, they are resistant to a cell-type-specific loss of GluClα.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7 where Mi1 and Tm3 specific GluClα knockdowns do not eliminate ON responses.

claim: ON selectivity is distributed across multiple synapses.
source: This shows that ON selectivity is distributed across multiple synapses, and raises the possibility that cell-type-specific manipulations might reveal similar strategies in other sensory systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of full mutant and cell-type-specific mutant results.

claim: Sensory coding is more distributed than predicted by simple circuit motifs.
source: Thus, sensory coding is more distributed than predicted by simple circuit motifs, allowing for robust neural processing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Distributed sensory coding allows for robust neural processing.
source: Thus, sensory coding is more distributed than predicted by simple circuit motifs, allowing for robust neural processing.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the distributed coding mechanism.

claim: Sensory systems sequentially extract increasingly complex features.
source: Sensory systems sequentially extract increasingly complex features.
evidence: This is a general principle of sensory processing cited from the literature.

claim: In the visual system, photoreceptors detect light and downstream neurons progressively extract distinct features such as contrast, direction of motion, form, or specific objects.
source: For example, in the visual system, photoreceptors detect light and then downstream neurons progressively extract distinct features, such as contrast, direction of motion, form, or specific objects (Gollisch and Meister, 2010; Livingstone and Hubel, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: ON/OFF dichotomy enables more efficient coding of stimuli in the visual system.
source: Such an ON/OFF dichotomy enables more efficient coding of stimuli in the visual system (Gjorgjieva et al., 2014) and occurs across many different species and sensory modalities, such as vision, olfaction, audition, thermosensation, and electrolocation (Bennett, 1971; Gallio et al., 2011; Scholl et al., 2010; Tichy and Hellwig, 2018; Werblin and Dowling, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: ON/OFF dichotomy occurs across many different species and sensory modalities including vision, olfaction, audition, thermosensation, and electrolocation.
source: Such an ON/OFF dichotomy enables more efficient coding of stimuli in the visual system (Gjorgjieva et al., 2014) and occurs across many different species and sensory modalities, such as vision, olfaction, audition, thermosensation, and electrolocation (Bennett, 1971; Gallio et al., 2011; Scholl et al., 2010; Tichy and Hellwig, 2018; Werblin and Dowling, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: In the vertebrate retina, ionotropic glutamate receptors on OFF bipolar cells maintain the sign of the response in the OFF pathway.
source: In the vertebrate retina, ON and OFF pathways split downstream of glutamatergic photoreceptors where ionotropic glutamate receptors on OFF bipolar cells maintain the sign of the response in the OFF pathway, and the metabotropic glutamate receptor mGluR6, located on ON bipolar cells, inverts the sign in the ON pathway (Koike et al., 2010; Masu et al., 1995; Vardi, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on vertebrate retina.

claim: The metabotropic glutamate receptor mGluR6, located on ON bipolar cells, inverts the sign in the ON pathway in the vertebrate retina.
source: In the vertebrate retina, ON and OFF pathways split downstream of glutamatergic photoreceptors where ionotropic glutamate receptors on OFF bipolar cells maintain the sign of the response in the OFF pathway, and the metabotropic glutamate receptor mGluR6, located on ON bipolar cells, inverts the sign in the ON pathway (Koike et al., 2010; Masu et al., 1995; Vardi, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on vertebrate retina.

claim: In the olfactory system of C. elegans, glutamate-gated chloride channels mediate the ON response.
source: In the olfactory system of C. elegans, an odor response can be split into parallel pathways in which glutamate-gated chloride channels mediate the ON response (Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature on C. elegans.

claim: Connectomics data reveals that neural circuits are intricate and many of the possible neuronal connections are realized.
source: While these transformations are thought to occur at specific synapses, connectomics data reveals that neural circuits are intricate and that many of the possible neuronal connections are realized (Eichler et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to connectomics studies.

claim: Important signal transformations might be distributed across wider circuit motifs.
source: This argues that important signal transformations might actually be distributed across wider circuit motifs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from connectomics data showing circuit complexity.

claim: In the Drosophila visual system, ON and OFF pathways functionally split in the first order lamina interneurons.
source: In the Drosophila visual system, ON and OFF pathways functionally split in the first order lamina interneurons, but the physiological specialization occurs one synaptic layer further downstream.
evidence: This is a description of the Drosophila visual system based on prior knowledge.

claim: The physiological specialization of ON and OFF pathways occurs one synaptic layer downstream of lamina interneurons.
source: In the Drosophila visual system, ON and OFF pathways functionally split in the first order lamina interneurons, but the physiological specialization occurs one synaptic layer further downstream.
evidence: This is a description of the Drosophila visual system based on prior knowledge.

claim: Information travels from the retina through three optic ganglia: the lamina, the medulla, and the lobula complex.
source: In brief, information travels from the retina, which houses the photoreceptors, through three optic ganglia: the lamina, the medulla, and the lobula complex, comprising lobula and lobula plate (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the anatomical organization shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Contrast is encoded by the transient response of photoreceptors.
source: Contrast is encoded by the transient response of photoreceptors, and downstream lamina neurons amplify the contrast-sensitive signal component (Laughlin, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Downstream lamina neurons amplify the contrast-sensitive signal component.
source: Contrast is encoded by the transient response of photoreceptors, and downstream lamina neurons amplify the contrast-sensitive signal component (Laughlin, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Distinct ON and OFF pathways are required to detect contrast increments and decrements, respectively.
source: Then, distinct ON and OFF pathways are required to detect contrast increments and decrements, respectively (Joesch et al., 2010; Strother et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: L1 is the major input to the ON pathway.
source: In the lamina, L1 is the major input to the ON pathway, whereas L2 and L3 feed into the OFF pathway (Clark et al., 2011; Joesch et al., 2010; Rister et al., 2007; Silies et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: L2 and L3 feed into the OFF pathway.
source: In the lamina, L1 is the major input to the ON pathway, whereas L2 and L3 feed into the OFF pathway (Clark et al., 2011; Joesch et al., 2010; Rister et al., 2007; Silies et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: All lamina neurons receiving direct input from photoreceptors depolarize to the offset of light and hyperpolarize to the onset of light.
source: However, all lamina neurons receiving direct input from photoreceptors depolarize to the offset of light and hyperpolarize to the onset of light (Clark et al., 2011; Laughlin, 1989; Silies et al., 2013; Uusitalo et al., 1995), thus passing on information about both ON and OFF (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lamina neurons pass on information about both ON and OFF.
source: However, all lamina neurons receiving direct input from photoreceptors depolarize to the offset of light and hyperpolarize to the onset of light (Clark et al., 2011; Laughlin, 1989; Silies et al., 2013; Uusitalo et al., 1995), thus passing on information about both ON and OFF (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the response properties and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Voltage or calcium signals in most downstream medulla neurons selectively report only one type of contrast polarity.
source: Voltage or calcium signals in most downstream medulla neurons then selectively report only one type of contrast polarity.
evidence: This is a general statement about medulla neuron properties based on prior knowledge.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 selectively respond with depolarization or an increase in calcium signal to ON.
source: The major ON pathway medulla neurons Mi1 and Tm3, for example, selectively respond with depolarization or an increase in calcium signal to ON (Figure 1B; Behnia et al., 2014; Strother et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In the OFF pathway, most neurons selectively respond to OFF stimuli, retaining the response polarity of their lamina inputs.
source: In the OFF pathway, most neurons instead selectively respond to OFF stimuli, retaining the response polarity of their lamina inputs (Figure 1B; Behnia et al., 2014; Serbe et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ON selectivity requires a sign inversion between the L1 input and its postsynaptic partners Mi1 and Tm3.
source: Therefore, ON selectivity requires a sign inversion between the L1 input and its postsynaptic partners Mi1 and Tm3.
evidence: This is inferred from the opposite response polarities of L1 versus Mi1/Tm3.

claim: The L1 input to the ON pathway is glutamatergic.
source: Previous work suggested that the L1 input to the ON pathway is glutamatergic, whereas L2 and L3, the two major inputs to the OFF pathway, are cholinergic (Davis et al., 2018; Takemura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: L2 and L3, the two major inputs to the OFF pathway, are cholinergic.
source: Previous work suggested that the L1 input to the ON pathway is glutamatergic, whereas L2 and L3, the two major inputs to the OFF pathway, are cholinergic (Davis et al., 2018; Takemura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Glutamate might be used as an inhibitory neurotransmitter to implement ON/OFF dichotomy in the fly visual system.
source: This suggests that glutamate might also be used as an inhibitory neurotransmitter to implement ON/OFF dichotomy in the fly visual system.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the neurotransmitter identities of lamina neurons.

claim: The molecular and cellular mechanisms implementing signal transformation in ON selectivity are not known in Drosophila visual circuitry.
source: However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms implementing this signal transformation are not known in Drosophila visual circuitry.
evidence: This establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: L1 makes the largest number of synapses with Mi1 and Tm3.
source: In the ON pathway, L1 makes the largest number of synapses with the medulla intrinsic Mi1 neuron and the transmedullary Tm3 interneurons (Figure 1A; Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to connectomics data and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: L1 has many other outputs besides Mi1 and Tm3.
source: However, L1 has many other outputs, and Mi1 and Tm3 many additional inputs, such as indirect L1 input via L5, or the GABAergic neuron C2, among others (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to connectomics data.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 have many additional inputs including indirect L1 input via L5 and the GABAergic neuron C2.
source: However, L1 has many other outputs, and Mi1 and Tm3 many additional inputs, such as indirect L1 input via L5, or the GABAergic neuron C2, among others (Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to connectomics data.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 medulla neurons project to T4, the first direction-selective cells of the ON pathway.
source: One synaptic layer downstream, Mi1 and Tm3 medulla neurons project to T4, the first direction-selective cells of the ON pathway (Figure 1A; Fisher et al., 2015a; Maisak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Genetic silencing of Mi1 or Tm3 leads to some deficits in ON edge motion detection.
source: While genetic silencing of Mi1 or Tm3 leads to some deficits in ON edge motion detection (Ammer et al., 2015; Strother et al., 2017), these flies are not ON motion blind, arguing that other neurons must also play a role in motion detection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Flies with silenced Mi1 or Tm3 are not ON motion blind.
source: While genetic silencing of Mi1 or Tm3 leads to some deficits in ON edge motion detection (Ammer et al., 2015; Strother et al., 2017), these flies are not ON motion blind, arguing that other neurons must also play a role in motion detection.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Other neurons besides Mi1 and Tm3 must play a role in motion detection.
source: While genetic silencing of Mi1 or Tm3 leads to some deficits in ON edge motion detection (Ammer et al., 2015; Strother et al., 2017), these flies are not ON motion blind, arguing that other neurons must also play a role in motion detection.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete loss of ON motion detection upon Mi1/Tm3 silencing.

claim: Mi4 and Mi9 have been added to the ON pathway.
source: Mi4 and Mi9 have now been added to the ON pathway (Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Mi4 and Mi9 are modulated by octopamine.
source: These cell types are modulated by octopamine, but silencing Mi4 or Mi9 individually has only subtle phenotypes (Strother et al., 2018; Strother et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Silencing Mi4 or Mi9 individually has only subtle phenotypes.
source: These cell types are modulated by octopamine, but silencing Mi4 or Mi9 individually has only subtle phenotypes (Strother et al., 2018; Strother et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In the OFF pathway, combinatorial block of more than one cell type aggravates behavioral deficits.
source: In the OFF pathway, combinatorial block of more than one cell type aggravates behavioral deficits (Fisher et al., 2015a; Serbe et al., 2016; Silies et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: L1 calcium signals are of the opposite sign to the calcium signal in Mi1 and Tm3.
source: L1 calcium signals (dark blue, n = 6 [99]) are of the opposite sign to the calcium signal in its major postsynaptic partners Mi1 (light blue, n = 5 [89]) and Tm3 (green, n = 7 [84]).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with calcium imaging data.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 dendrites show an increase in iGluSnFR signal in response to light OFF and a decrease in response to light ON.
source: In M1 and M5, both Mi1 and Tm3 neurons showed an increase in iGluSnFR signal in response to light OFF and a decrease in iGluSnFR signal in response to light ON, showing that rectification happens downstream of the glutamatergic input (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C,D with iGluSnFR imaging data.

claim: Rectification happens downstream of the glutamatergic input to Mi1 and Tm3.
source: In M1 and M5, both Mi1 and Tm3 neurons showed an increase in iGluSnFR signal in response to light OFF and a decrease in iGluSnFR signal in response to light ON, showing that rectification happens downstream of the glutamatergic input (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is inferred from the iGluSnFR signals showing non-rectified glutamate release.

claim: iGluSnFR signals on Mi1 and Tm3 dendrites were of the same polarity as intracellular calcium signals recorded within the presynaptic L1 axon terminals.
source: These signals were of the same polarity as intracellular calcium signals recorded within the presynaptic L1 axon terminals, and of the opposite polarity to calcium signals in the same layers of Mi1 and Tm3 (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing data in Figures 1B-D.

claim: iGluSnFR signals on Mi1 and Tm3 dendrites were of the opposite polarity to calcium signals in the same layers of Mi1 and Tm3.
source: These signals were of the same polarity as intracellular calcium signals recorded within the presynaptic L1 axon terminals, and of the opposite polarity to calcium signals in the same layers of Mi1 and Tm3 (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing data in Figures 1B-D.

claim: In the proximal medulla (layer M9/10), Mi1 and Tm3 showed weak iGluSnFR signals that increased in response to both light ON and OFF.
source: In the proximal medulla (layer M9/10), Mi1 and Tm3 neurons showed weak iGluSnFR signals that increased in response to both light ON and OFF (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C,D with iGluSnFR imaging data.

claim: The major postsynaptic targets of L1 receive glutamatergic input that provides information about both ON and OFF signals.
source: This data shows that the major postsynaptic targets of L1 receive glutamatergic input that provides information about both ON and OFF signals, which is in line with graded inputs coming from the L1 input to the ON pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the iGluSnFR data showing non-rectified glutamate signals.

claim: Other glutamatergic inputs might further shape medulla neuron properties in the proximal medulla.
source: Other glutamatergic inputs might further shape medulla neuron properties in the proximal medulla.
evidence: This is speculation based on the iGluSnFR signals in M9/10.

claim: Glutamatergic inhibition can be mediated by metabotropic glutamate receptors or by ionotropic glutamate-gated chloride channels.
source: Glutamatergic inhibition can be mediated either by metabotropic glutamate receptors or by ionotropic glutamate-gated chloride channels (Collins et al., 2012; Cully et al., 1996; Liu and Wilson, 2013; Parmentier et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mi1 shows a transient increase in calcium signals in response to the ON step that decays to reach a plateau response within 2 s.
source: When flies expressing GCaMP6f in Mi1 neurons were shown 5 s full-field flashes, Mi1 showed a transient increase in calcium signals in response to the ON step that decayed to reach a plateau response within 2 s (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A with calcium imaging data.

claim: MPEP, a selective blocker of metabotropic glutamate receptors, did not reduce the responses to visual light flashes in Mi1 neurons.
source: Bath application of 2-Methyl-6-(phenylethenyl) pyridine hydrochloride (MPEP), a selective blocker of metabotropic glutamate receptors, to the same flies did not reduce the responses to visual light flashes in Mi1 neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B with pharmacological data.

claim: Tm3 responses were not affected by MPEP application.
source: Similar to Mi1, Tm3 responses were not affected by MPEP application (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D with pharmacological data.

claim: Picrotoxin is known to inhibit glutamate-gated chloride channels at high concentrations.
source: We next applied picrotoxin (PTX), a drug that is known to inhibit glutamate-gated chloride channels at high concentrations (Cully et al., 1996; Etter et al., 1999), but which also affects GABAARs at much lower concentration (Takeuchi and Takeuchi, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Picrotoxin affects GABAARs at much lower concentration than glutamate-gated chloride channels.
source: We next applied picrotoxin (PTX), a drug that is known to inhibit glutamate-gated chloride channels at high concentrations (Cully et al., 1996; Etter et al., 1999), but which also affects GABAARs at much lower concentration (Takeuchi and Takeuchi, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: 1–5 μM PTX was used to effectively block GABA-gated hyperpolarization in the olfactory system and GABAergic inhibition in Drosophila visual system neurons.
source: In vivo studies in Drosophila had previously used concentrations of 1–5 μM PTX to effectively block GABA-gated hyperpolarization in the olfactory system and GABAergic inhibition in Drosophila visual system neurons (Fisher et al., 2015b; Wilson and Laurent, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: 100 μM PTX was used to block GluCls in the olfactory system.
source: In contrast, 100 μM PTX was used to block GluCls in the olfactory system (Liu and Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Upon bath application of 100 μM PTX, visual responses were completely abolished in Mi1 neurons.
source: Upon bath application of 100 μM PTX, visual responses were completely abolished in Mi1 neurons (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with pharmacological data.

claim: When 2.5 μM PTX was applied, ON responses were also lost in Mi1.
source: Surprisingly, when we tested the effect of low concentrations (2.5 μM) of PTX, ON responses were also lost in Mi1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with pharmacological data.

claim: Visual responses were lost at PTX concentrations ranging from 2.5 μM to 100 μM in Mi1.
source: To test this effect more precisely, we used a range of PTX concentrations and observed a loss of visual responses at concentrations ranging from 2.5 μM to 100 μM PTX in Mi1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B with dose-response data.

claim: All ON responses were eliminated in Tm3 at 100 μM PTX and strongly reduced at low concentrations of PTX.
source: When we performed the same experiments in Tm3, we again found all ON responses to be eliminated in 100 μM PTX and strongly reduced at low concentrations of PTX (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C,D with pharmacological data.

claim: The PTX effect on Mi1 and Tm3 was consistent across all medulla layers.
source: This effect was consistent across all medulla layers (Figure 2A–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 with data from multiple layers.

claim: Dendritic Mi1 and Tm3 regions showed a small decrease in calcium in response to light at the highest PTX concentrations.
source: Dendritic Mi1 and Tm3 regions even showed a small decrease in calcium in response to light at the highest PTX concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D with calcium imaging data.

claim: T4/T5 neurons hardly showed any response to full-field flashes before toxin application, due to surround inhibition.
source: When we measured flash responses in T4/T5 cells expressing GCaMP6f, these neurons hardly showed any response to full-field flashes before toxin application, due to surround inhibition (Figure 2E,F; Fisher et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E,F and supported by a citation.

claim: Upon bath application of 2.5 μM PTX, T4/T5 flash responses were disinhibited, and T4/T5 neurons responded with an increase in calcium signal to both light ON and OFF.
source: Upon bath application of 2.5 μM PTX, these flash responses were disinhibited, and T4/T5 neurons responded with an increase in calcium signal to both light ON and OFF (Figure 2E,F; Fisher et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E,F with pharmacological data.

claim: T4/T5 neurons still show flash responses under conditions in which all responses of their predominant Mi1 and Tm3 inputs are abolished.
source: Thus, T4/T5 neurons still show flash responses under conditions in which all responses of their predominant Mi1 and Tm3 inputs are abolished (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing T4/T5 responses at 2.5 μM PTX with Mi1/Tm3 responses at the same concentration.

claim: At least under low PTX concentrations, other neurons and a lack of local inhibition can contribute to T4 responses.
source: This suggests, that at least under low PTX concentrations, other neurons (Takemura et al., 2017) and a lack of local inhibition (Mauss et al., 2015) can contribute to T4 responses.
evidence: This is inferred from T4/T5 responses persisting when Mi1/Tm3 are blocked, supported by citations.

claim: After increasing the concentration of PTX to 100 μM, all ON responses were abolished in T4/T5.
source: After increasing the concentration of PTX to 100 μM within the same fly, all ON responses were abolished (Figure 2E,F), showing that T4 no longer receives any functional inputs at high PTX concentrations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E,F with pharmacological data.

claim: T4 no longer receives any functional inputs at high PTX concentrations.
source: After increasing the concentration of PTX to 100 μM within the same fly, all ON responses were abolished (Figure 2E,F), showing that T4 no longer receives any functional inputs at high PTX concentrations.
evidence: This is inferred from the complete loss of ON responses in T4/T5 at 100 μM PTX.

claim: OFF responses in T4/T5 were unaffected by 100 μM PTX relative to the 2.5 μM phenotype.
source: In contrast, OFF responses were unaffected relative to the 2.5 μM phenotype (Figure 2E,F), arguing that the effect on the ON pathway is specific.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E,F with pharmacological data.

claim: The PTX effect on the ON pathway is specific.
source: In contrast, OFF responses were unaffected relative to the 2.5 μM phenotype (Figure 2E,F), arguing that the effect on the ON pathway is specific.
evidence: This is inferred from OFF responses being unaffected while ON responses are abolished.

claim: The PTX effect is consistent with glutamate-gated chloride channels mediating ON responses in the visual system.
source: This is in line with the idea that glutamate-gated chloride channels mediate ON responses in the visual system.
evidence: This is inferred from the ON-specific effect of PTX.

claim: The L1 input still responded to visual stimuli even at the highest PTX concentrations used.
source: Importantly, the L1 input still responded to visual stimuli even at the highest PTX concentrations used (Figure 2G,H) and the iGluSnFR signal on the dendrites of Mi1 or Tm3 were largely unaltered, or even slightly increased at concentrations at which all Mi1 and Tm3 calcium responses were abolished (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), demonstrating that the glutamatergic input to the ON pathway was still intact.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The iGluSnFR signal on the dendrites of Mi1 or Tm3 were largely unaltered, or even slightly increased at PTX concentrations at which all Mi1 and Tm3 calcium responses were abolished.
source: Importantly, the L1 input still responded to visual stimuli even at the highest PTX concentrations used (Figure 2G,H) and the iGluSnFR signal on the dendrites of Mi1 or Tm3 were largely unaltered, or even slightly increased at concentrations at which all Mi1 and Tm3 calcium responses were abolished (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), demonstrating that the glutamatergic input to the ON pathway was still intact.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The glutamatergic input to the ON pathway was still intact at PTX concentrations that abolished Mi1 and Tm3 responses.
source: Importantly, the L1 input still responded to visual stimuli even at the highest PTX concentrations used (Figure 2G,H) and the iGluSnFR signal on the dendrites of Mi1 or Tm3 were largely unaltered, or even slightly increased at concentrations at which all Mi1 and Tm3 calcium responses were abolished (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), demonstrating that the glutamatergic input to the ON pathway was still intact.
evidence: This is inferred from L1 responses and iGluSnFR signals persisting during PTX application.

claim: A systemic disruption of glutamate-gated chloride channels abolishes ON responses in Mi1 and Tm3.
source: Taken together, our findings show that a systemic disruption of glutamate-gated chloride channels abolishes ON responses in Mi1 and Tm3, and suggest that GABAA receptors might play a role in mediating ON responses at the L1 to Mi1/Tm3 synapses in the fly visual system.
evidence: This is the conclusion from the PTX experiments.

claim: GABAA receptors might play a role in mediating ON responses at the L1 to Mi1/Tm3 synapses in the fly visual system.
source: Taken together, our findings show that a systemic disruption of glutamate-gated chloride channels abolishes ON responses in Mi1 and Tm3, and suggest that GABAA receptors might play a role in mediating ON responses at the L1 to Mi1/Tm3 synapses in the fly visual system.
evidence: This is inferred from the low-concentration PTX effects and will be tested with PTX-insensitive alleles.

claim: The only glutamate-gated chloride channel in the fly genome is encoded by the GluClα gene.
source: The only glutamate-gated chloride channel in the fly genome is encoded by the GluClα gene.
evidence: This is a statement about the Drosophila genome.

claim: A GluClα protein tagged with GFP (GluClαMI02890.GFSTF.2) was found to be widely expressed in the visual system, including the lamina, medulla, lobula and lobula plate.
source: A GluClα protein tagged with GFP (GluClαMI02890.GFSTF.2) was found to be widely expressed in the visual system, including the lamina, medulla, lobula and lobula plate (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with immunohistochemistry data.

claim: GluClα expression was stronger in some proximal medulla layers.
source: Expression was stronger in some proximal medulla layers, but the broad expression of this GFP trap did not allow expression to be assigned to specific cell types (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with immunohistochemistry data.

claim: GluClα mRNA was strongly expressed in all major ON pathway medulla neurons: Mi1, Tm3, Mi4, and Mi9.
source: GluClα mRNA was strongly expressed in all major ON pathway medulla neurons: Mi1, Tm3, Mi4, and Mi9 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with RNA-seq data.

claim: GluClα was also expressed in OFF pathway neurons (Tm1, Tm2, Tm4, and Tm9), albeit weaker in Tm9.
source: Furthermore, GluClα was also expressed in OFF pathway neurons (Tm1, Tm2, Tm4, and Tm9), albeit weaker in Tm9 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

source: The fact that the RdlMDRR allele does not fully rescue all ON responses in Mi1 or Tm3 suggests that PTX might also be acting on GluClα in this context.

claim: Responses in medulla neurons Mi1 and Tm3 are mediated at least in part by the GABAA receptor Rdl.

claim: There is no evidence for L1 co-releasing GABA in addition to glutamate.

claim: A GABAergic synapse involving Rdl is likely involved in circuitry upstream of Mi1 and Tm3.
source: This suggests that visual responses to ON stimuli in Mi1 and Tm3 do not arise solely through a monosynaptic connection with the L1 inputs as previously thought (Figure 4Gi), but that a GABAergic synapse involving Rdl is likely involved in circuitry upstream of Mi1 and Tm3.
evidence: This is inferred from the Rdl rescue and the lack of evidence for L1 being GABAergic.

claim: Rdl-dependent circuits parallel to the glutamatergic L1 to medulla neuron synapse can mediate ON responses.

evidence: This establishes the need to generate a PTX-insensitive GluClα allele.

source: We next wanted to test if and to what degree GluClα contributes to visual ON responses. evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: PTX interacts with specific residues of the M2 transmembrane alpha helix of GluClα.
source: PTX interacts with specific residues of the M2 transmembrane alpha helix (Figure 5A; Hibbs and Gouaux, 2011).

claim: The M2 region of ligand-gated chloride channels is highly conserved among different channels and among species, with the exception of a single variable amino acid corresponding to S278 in D. melanogaster GluClα.
source: This region is highly conserved among different channels and among species, with the exception of a single variable amino acid, corresponding to amino acid S278 in D. melanogaster GluClα (red, Figure 5B).

claim: The identity of amino acid S278 in GluClα correlates strongly with the PTX sensitivity of the channel.
source: The identity of this single amino acid correlates strongly with the PTX sensitivity of the channel (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with sequence alignment and PTX sensitivity data.

claim: Mutations in amino acid S278 have been shown to change the PTX sensitivity of ligand-gated chloride channels.
source: Mutations in this amino acid have been shown to change the PTX sensitivity of the channel.
evidence: This is general knowledge about ligand-gated chloride channels.

claim: The A > S substitution in the D. melanogaster GABAAR allele RdlMDRR exhibits reduced sensitivity to PTX.
source: For example, the A > S substitution in the D. melanogaster GABAAR allele RdlMDRR exhibits reduced sensitivity to PTX (Figure 4, Ffrench-Constant et al., 1993; Fisher et al., 2015a).

claim: A GluClαS278T mutant was generated to create a potentially PTX-insensitive version of GluClα.

evidence: This describes the generation of the mutant allele.

claim: Wild type GluClα-expressing oocytes revealed fast activating and rapidly inactivating glutamate-induced currents.

claim: Wild type GluClα current was sensitive to PTX.

claim: The glutamate-induced currents in the GluClαS278T mutant were insensitive to PTX.
source: Importantly, the glutamate-induced currents in the GluClαS278T mutant were insensitive to PTX (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D,E with electrophysiology data.

claim: GluClαS278T flies responded to visual stimuli with the typical peak and plateau response in the absence of toxin.
source: In the absence of toxin, GluClαS278T flies responded to visual stimuli with the typical peak and plateau response, arguing that the altered kinetics of the GluClαS278T mutant observed in oocytes was not a problem under these stimulus conditions (Figure 6A,B).

claim: Upon application of 2.5 μM PTX, calcium responses were lost in Mi1 neurons of heterozygous GluClα controls.

claim: In flies only expressing the GluClαS278T and no wild type protein, the ON responses were partially rescued at 2.5 μM PTX.
source: In flies only expressing the GluClαS278T and no wild type protein, the ON responses were partially rescued.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: The rescue by GluClαS278T was specifically prominent for the step response, which was significantly rescued in all medulla layers.
source: The rescue was specifically prominent for the step response, which was significantly rescued by GluClαS278T in all medulla layers (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C with quantification.

claim: GluClα in vivo is sensitive to lower concentrations of PTX than previously thought.
source: This shows that GluClα in vivo is sensitive to lower concentrations of PTX than previously thought, arguing that there is no specific concentrations to only block Rdl, and highlighting the usefulness of these PTX-insensitive alleles for molecular specificity.
evidence: This is inferred from the GluClαS278T rescue at 2.5 μM PTX.

claim: The rescue by GluClαS278T demonstrates that GluClα mediates ON responses in Mi1 in the fly visual system.
source: Furthermore, the rescue by GluClαS278T demonstrates that GluClα mediates ON responses in Mi1 in the fly visual system.
evidence: This is the conclusion from the GluClαS278T rescue experiments.

claim: The integrated ON response in Tm3 was significantly rescued by GluClαS278T in layer M1 at 2.5 μM PTX.
source: The integrated ON response was still significantly rescued in a GluClαS278T background in layer M1 (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6E,F with quantification.

claim: In other medulla layers, 2.5 μM PTX more prominently blocked the peak Tm3 ON response in controls, but not in a GluClαS278T-insensitive background.
source: In other medulla layers, 2.5 μM PTX more prominently blocked the peak Tm3 ON response in controls, but not in a GluClαS278T-insensitive background (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: GluClαS278T mediates ON responses in Tm3.

source: At high concentrations of PTX (100 μM), the PTX-insensitive GluClαS278T allele did not rescue ON responses in either Mi1 or Tm3 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–L).

claim: GluClαS278T rescued the 100 μM PTX phenotype in T4/T5.
source: To test if GluClαS278T can rescue T4/T5 responses at high concentrations, we recorded calcium signals in T4/T5 cells in a GluClαS278T background. Indeed, ON responses to full-field light flashes in 100 μM PTX were rescued (Figure 6G–I).

claim: GluClαS278T can be effective to rescue responses in some cell types at high PTX concentrations in vivo.
source: Thus, the use of the toxin-insensitive GluClαS278T mutant demonstrates that GluClα also mediates ON responses in vivo in the fly visual system.
evidence: This is the conclusion from the T4/T5 rescue at 100 μM PTX.

claim: The use of the toxin-insensitive GluClαS278T mutant demonstrates that GluClα mediates ON responses in vivo in the fly visual system.
source: Thus, the use of the toxin-insensitive GluClαS278T mutant demonstrates that GluClα also mediates ON responses in vivo in the fly visual system.
evidence: This is the conclusion from all GluClαS278T rescue experiments.

claim: Both glutamatergic and GABAergic inhibition play a combinatorial role in mediating ON responses.
source: Together, our data provides support for a combinatorial role of glutamatergic and GABAergic inhibition in mediating ON responses.
evidence: This is the conclusion from both Rdl and GluClα experiments.

claim: GluClα is likely to be the receptor on all neurons postsynaptic to L1.
source: Because of the glutamatergic L1 input, GluClα is likely to be the receptor on all neurons postsynaptic to L1 (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is inferred from L1 being glutamatergic and GluClα being required for ON responses.

claim: Rdl could function downstream of GluClα.
source: Rdl could function downstream of GluClα.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental results.

claim: A pathway parallel to a monosynaptic glutamatergic circuit can mediate ON responses in Mi1 and Tm3.
source: This suggests that a pathway parallel to a monosynaptic glutamatergic circuit can also mediate ON responses in Mi1 and Tm3 (Figure 6J).
evidence: This is the model proposed based on the experimental results, shown in Figure 6J.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 responses might not depend solely on monosynaptic L1 input if there is no evidence for L1 being GABAergic.
source: Given that there is no evidence for L1 being GABAergic, Mi1 and Tm3 responses might not depend solely on monosynaptic L1 input.
evidence: This is inferred from the Rdl requirement and L1 not being GABAergic.

claim: Mi1 and Tm3 might still be able to respond to ON signals when GluClα function is only disrupted within the respective cell type.
source: If this hypothesis is correct, GluClα should not exclusively function in a cell-autonomous manner in neurons downstream of L1, suggesting that Mi1 and Tm3 might still be able to respond to ON signals when GluClα function is only disrupted within the respective cell type.
evidence: This is the prediction being tested with cell-type-specific manipulations.

claim: GluClαFlpStop.D is a full loss of function allele.
source: Upon pan-neuronal inversion of the FlpStop cassette into the non-disrupting orientation (GluClαFlpStop.D) quantification of GluClα expression levels using qRT-PCR showed that transcription was disrupted by half when the FlpStop exon was inverted in a heterozygous background, arguing for a full loss of function in GluClαFlpStop.D (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is inferred from the qRT-PCR data showing 50% reduction in heterozygotes.

claim: When GluClα was disrupted specifically in Mi1 neurons, visual responses to ON flashes were still present in Mi1 neurons and did not differ from controls.

evidence: This is shown in Figure 7E,F with calcium imaging data.

claim: ON responses are not mediated monosynaptically, but pathways parallel to the L1-Mi1 or L1-Tm3 connection might be sufficient to mediate ON responses.
source: These results demonstrate that ON selectivity is not mediated monosynaptically, but that pathways parallel to the L1-Mi1 or L1-Tm3 connection might be sufficient to mediate ON responses.
evidence: This is the conclusion from the cell-type-specific GluClα loss-of-function experiments.

claim: All ON responses might still depend on GluClα at the first synapse postsynaptic to L1.

source: GluClαFlpStop.D mutant flies eclosed but showed locomotor deficits.
evidence: This is an observation about the mutant phenotype.

claim: Normal ON responses are not lost when GluClα is disrupted in a cell-type-specific manner.
source: Thus, normal ON responses are lost whenever GluClα function is disrupted in the entire visual system, but not when it is disrupted in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: This is the conclusion from comparing full mutant and cell-type-specific mutant results.

claim: ON selectivity is a multisynaptic computation that is robust to perturbations at individual synapses.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that ON selectivity is a multisynaptic computation that is robust to perturbations at individual synapses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the GluClα experiments.
